method: Same-agent English/Marathi close reading and reverse paraphrase; not independent or human review.
scope: All six translated content blocks on the alternative pairing construction, its closed formula, codes and a non-surjective encoding.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Fill positive-integer positions with row 0 in alternating empty cells, then repeat within the remaining cells for rows 1, 2, 3 and onward.
samples.checks: The ordering and all three displayed tables are preserved; OLSIZ-004 and OLSIZ-005 make the two inconsistent source labels explicit.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Row 0 occupies odd positions, row 1 twice odd positions, row 2 four times odd positions, so pair 〈n,m〉 has one-based position 2^n(2m+1).
samples.checks: Row indices, odd factors, powers, exponent-coordinate relation and formula are unchanged.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Subtracting one converts the one-based position to a natural-number code, giving h(n,m)=2^n(2m+1)-1.
samples.checks: The zero-based adjustment, domain, codomain and pairing-function claim remain exact.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The example codes are 0 for 〈0,0〉, 9 for 〈1,2〉 and 51 for 〈2,6〉.
samples.checks: Each substitution and arithmetic equality is byte-structurally preserved.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: An injective encoding need not be surjective and then has only a partial inverse; j(n,m)=2^n3^m is such an injection into positive naturals and hence into naturals.
samples.checks: The distinction between injection and surjection, the partial-inverse consequence, both codomains and the formula are preserved.

limitations: T072 groups elementary number vocabulary whose exact Marathi labels were not newly externally attested before current use.
No independent linguistic certification has been performed.
